tier_reason: First-party blog post by the author (csjh.blog, blocked here); WebSearch snippets of the post relay a startup table (hyperfine, M1 MacBook Air) with the in-place interpreter at 35.4 ms versus Wasmtime 183.3 ms on SpiderMonkey, matching the record. No benchmark code, compiler version or exact build flags are public (repo Makefile release target is clang++ -O2 -std=c++20, but the post's build is not known), so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Snippet only (search-result relay of the post's startup table, hyperfine on an M1 MacBook Air, ms): SpiderMonkey 35.4 (in-place interpreter) vs 183.3 (Wasmtime) vs 197.4 (Wasmtime single-pass) vs 66.3 (Node), about 5.2x faster than Wasmtime (derived from page data); esbuild 64.7 vs 209.9 (Wasmtime) vs 75.3 (Node); Figma 108.3 vs 710.4 (Wasmtime) vs 92.5 (Node, faster than the interpreter). Validation alone takes 24.8 ms on SpiderMonkey. Execution speed is far slower than Wasmtime: Coremark 749.6 vs 28260.4 (higher is better, about 38x slower, derived from page data), SpiderMonkey score about 2.83 vs 577, esbuild 'too slow' to report.
corrections.hardware: Apple M1 MacBook Air (snippet only: the post says startup was timed with hyperfine on an M1 MacBook Air).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the blog numbers. The repo Makefile builds with clang++ (-std=c++20; release target adds -O2).
corrections.caveats: Snippet only: csjh.blog is blocked by the egress proxy (EGRESS_BLOCKED), so the numbers come from WebSearch summaries of the post's tables, not from the page itself. The repo README is a single heading and holds no benchmark code. The win is startup only (load, validate, instantiate): the interpreter is roughly 38x slower than Wasmtime on Coremark execution (derived from page data), about 200x lower on the SpiderMonkey score, and too slow to finish esbuild; Node starts the largest binary (Figma) faster (92.5 vs 108.3 ms). Wasmtime startup here includes its up-front Cranelift compile of the whole module (cache settings unknown); Wasmtime's own Pulley interpreter was not compared. Single machine (M1), compiler and flags of the measured build unknown. Last commit 2025-07-15 (merged trunc_sat spec fix), so stale.

notes: Startup claim (35.4 vs 183.3 ms SpiderMonkey) matches the post's table as relayed by search snippets; tier stays C. Shortcomings: snippet-only evidence from a blocked first-party blog, no benchmark code in repo, startup-only win while execution is about 38x slower than Wasmtime on Coremark, and Node beats it on startup of the largest binary (Figma).

tier_reason: First-party blog post (csjh.blog, blocked here) relayed by WebSearch snippets: startup table (hyperfine, M1 MacBook Air) and execution table against Wasmtime, Wasmtime single-pass and Node. No benchmark code or build flags in the repo, so C.

corrections.workload: Two Arm64 macOS JIT backends in one repo: the 'minimal' unrolled-interpreter JIT (backend/arm64/minimal.cpp) and the 'baseline' single-pass JIT (backend/arm64/baseline.cpp). The author's blog post 'A Tale of Three WebAssembly Runtimes' times startup (load, validate, instantiate) of SpiderMonkey, esbuild and Figma Wasm binaries with hyperfine, and execution speed on esbuild, SpiderMonkey and Coremark, against Wasmtime (default and single-pass) and Node.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Snippet only (search-result relay of the post's tables, M1 MacBook Air). Startup, ms: SpiderMonkey 52.8 (unrolled JIT) and 65.8 (single-pass JIT) vs 183.3 (Wasmtime), 197.4 (Wasmtime single-pass), 66.3 (Node); esbuild 89.8 / 102.0 vs 209.9 / 243.6 / 75.3; Figma 159.7 / 198.8 vs 710.4 / 767.5 / 92.5 (Node faster on esbuild and Figma). Execution: the 'beats Node and Wasmtime on esbuild' result belongs to the single-pass (baseline) JIT, 3.126 s vs Wasmtime 3.316 s (1.06x) and Node 3.694 s (1.18x) (derived from page data); the unrolled JIT was 'too slow' for esbuild. Single-pass JIT loses to Wasmtime on SpiderMonkey score (347 vs 577) and Coremark (26616.0 vs 28260.4) but beats Node on both (300, 24853.7); the unrolled JIT scores 11.8 and 1326.6, about 21x below Wasmtime on Coremark (derived from page data).
corrections.hardware: Apple M1 MacBook Air (snippet only); the README says only Arm64 on macOS is expected to work.
corrections.caveats: Snippet only: csjh.blog is blocked by the egress proxy (EGRESS_BLOCKED); numbers come from WebSearch summaries of the post's tables. The record attributed the esbuild win to the unrolled JIT, but per the post it is the single-pass (baseline) backend, and only by 1.06x over Wasmtime; that backend is slower than Wasmtime on SpiderMonkey (347 vs 577) and Coremark (26616 vs 28260). The unrolled JIT wins only on startup and is about 21x slower than Wasmtime on Coremark execution (derived from page data). Node starts esbuild and Figma faster than both JITs. No benchmark code, compiler flags or build file (no Makefile or CMakeLists.txt at the repo root) are public; README says 'Not meant for production use'. No LICENSE file in the repository, so usability is reference. Arm64 macOS only; one machine.

notes: Numbers relayed by search snippets match the record's startup figures (52.8 vs 183.3 ms SpiderMonkey); the esbuild win (3.126 vs 3.316 s Wasmtime, 3.694 s Node) belongs to the single-pass baseline backend, not the unrolled JIT, so claim and workload were corrected; tier stays C. Shortcomings: snippet-only first-party evidence, no license, Arm64 macOS only, execution win over Wasmtime on 1 of 3 workloads and only 1.06x.

tier_reason: README benchmarks section shows first-party PNG bar charts (wasm3 vs miniwasm, 2020 MacBook Air M1, emcc -O2, bench.py and test/bench/*.c public); my readings of the charts match the record. Not A: the wasm3 baseline's version and build are unstated, the compiler version is unstated, each test ran once, and the charts (commit 70dd3e6, 2023-01-09) cannot be regenerated from current HEAD because bench.py and the makefile changed.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Benchmark wasm modules built with emcc -O2 (bench.py default; no extra emcc flags). README build line is 'make CC=gcc' ('gcc is fastest in my tests'); at the chart commit 70dd3e6 (2023-01-09) the makefile default was OPT ?= -O2 for compile and link. The wasm3 version and build flags, and the gcc/clang version, are not stated. The CI workflow (.github/workflows/all.yml) uses OPT='-O3 -flto -fomit-frame-pointer' and wasm3 built from source with cmake on ubuntu-latest, but the README charts are from the M1 laptop, not CI.
corrections.caveats: Numbers exist only as PNG bar charts (my visual readings, not page text), each benchmark was run once by default (bench.py runs=1; wall-clock time.time() around a subprocess, so process start and module load are included), on one M1 laptop with no noise control. Margins on coremark (about 1.06x) and mandelbrot (about 1.1x) are within laptop run-to-run noise; only fib_i32, binary-trees and fannkuch-redux show clear gaps. Executing a trap is about 5x slower than wasm3. The charts date from commit 70dd3e6 (2023-01-09); the interpreter was reworked afterwards (new block system, f64 ops, simde, through May 2023), so they do not describe current code. Current HEAD cannot reproduce them as-is: bench.py now always appends wasmer and wasmtime and has coremark commented out, and the makefile has a typo ('CLAGS_opt = -O3' instead of CFLAGS_opt), so the default build compiles miniwasm without any -O flag. README says the wasm spec test suite is only ~75% complete, so miniwasm is not a fully conformant engine, unlike wasm3. No claim against wasmtime, wasmer, WAMR or V8 is published; CI chart artifacts are not available. The Hacker News thread was not readable here (HN blocked).

notes: Chart values confirmed by viewing res/*.png (wasm3 vs miniwasm, fib_i32 3.0 vs 1.17 s etc.); tier stays C (borderline A on code/flags/CPU, held at C because the wasm3 baseline build is unstated and the charts predate a rewrite). Shortcomings: chart-only single-run numbers, trap 5x slower, ~75% spec-test pass rate, current makefile typo builds without optimisation, no comparison with the category baselines (wasmtime, wasmer, WAMR, V8).
